scenes.text: Look at the biggest question parts in the last five years of HSC Chemistry and Biology papers, the ones worth seven marks or more. Of the seventeen that used a glossary key word, ten asked you to analyse, evaluate or justify. And in seven of the last twelve marking feedback reports, NESA flagged the same weakness: a judgement without enough reasons from the evidence. So let's learn to make a call, and back it up.

Here's what NESA's glossary says, in short. Analyse means break something into parts, show how they connect, and work out what follows. Assess means judge the value, quality, outcomes, results or size of something. Evaluate means judge against criteria, or work out the value. Justify means give support for an argument or a conclusion. Three of them end in a judgement, a call you make or support. All four need reasons.

Here's an HSC-style Chemistry question. About fifty millilitres of one mole per litre hydrochloric acid has spilled on a lab bench. You could neutralise it with calcium carbonate powder, or with sodium hydroxide solution. A table compares them. The question asks you to evaluate using calcium carbonate rather than sodium hydroxide. Four marks. If you take Biology, watch the shape of the answer: your question is coming.

Run the routine. The verb is evaluate, so you'll end with a judgement, tested against criteria. Four marks suggests about four linked points. The phrase rather than sodium hydroxide is a constraint: every point weighs one against the other. And the table rows are your evidence: use them, don't just copy them.

An assess or evaluate answer needs three parts. A verdict: your judgement, how good or how suitable. Criteria: what you're judging by. Here that's safety, what an excess does, and knowing when to stop. And evidence: the details from the question that show each one. Here's the memory aid: no verdict without a reason, and no reason without evidence.

Start with the verdict, so the marker knows where you're going: calcium carbonate is the more suitable choice. Then criterion one, safety. Calcium carbonate is low hazard, whereas sodium hydroxide is corrosive to skin and eyes. Criterion two, what happens if you add too much. Calcium carbonate is insoluble, so extra just sits there as a solid, and the mixture stays near pH eight. Extra sodium hydroxide would leave a strongly basic spill, above pH twelve.

Criterion three, knowing when to stop. Calcium carbonate fizzes as it reacts, and the fizzing stops when the acid is used up. Sodium hydroxide gives no sign. Now weigh a limitation, because a fair evaluation looks both ways: calcium carbonate is slower, and it gives off carbon dioxide. Then close the loop. For a small spill, safety and control matter more than speed, so calcium carbonate is the better choice. That's four.

Now here's a weaker answer. "Calcium carbonate is better than sodium hydroxide because it is safer and it is a weak base." There's a verdict, and even a because. But "safer" never says why, and nothing comes from the table. Weak base is true, but it never says why that matters here. In our marking guide it earns one of four, for a relevant judgement. It announces the answer without earning it.

NESA's marking guidelines show both halves matter. In one recent six-mark evaluate question, a judgement first appears at four marks, and the top bands asked for an informed judgement, based on analysis of the data. In a four-mark evaluate question, describing the effects for both cases reached three. Only evaluating them reached four. In both, answers without a judgement stopped short of the top, and no band paid for a verdict on its own.

So how is assess different from evaluate? They overlap: both need a supported judgement. Evaluate leans on criteria: name what you judge by, and weigh strengths against limitations. Assess leans on how much, or how good: you'd lead with how suitable, and how far. Either way, write all three parts. Justify asks for the support: whether the conclusion is given or you choose it, back it with reasons from the case. In one recent justify question, identifying two changes earned the same as fully justifying one. The reason was worth as much as a second change.

Your turn. Do the one in your subject, or both. Chemistry first. A buffer with a pH of about four point eight is needed. Ethanoic acid has a pKa of four point seven four. The ammonium ion has a pKa of nine point two five. Justify which acid, with its conjugate base, should be used to make the buffer. Two marks. Pause here to answer.

Verdict: ethanoic acid with ethanoate. Reason: a buffer works best when its pH is close to the acid's pKa, because then the acid and its conjugate base are in similar amounts, ready for added acid or base. Evidence: four point seven four is almost exactly four point eight, but nine point two five is over four units away. The habit to drop: "its pKa is closer," with no reason why closer matters.

Now Biology. Part of an mRNA sequence has the codon G A A, for glutamic acid. Mutation one changes it to G A G, still glutamic acid. Mutation two changes it to U A A, a stop codon. A student claims that a substitution mutation always changes the protein. Using the information, assess this claim. Three marks. Pause here to answer.

Verdict first: the claim is not supported, because of the word always. Mutation one gives G A G, still glutamic acid, so the protein stays the same. Mutation two makes a stop codon, so translation ends early and the polypeptide is shorter. Some substitutions change the protein, and some don't. The habit to drop: labelling them silent and nonsense, then stopping. That never judges the claim.

So, when you see one of these verbs. For assess or evaluate, make a judgement and support it with relevant criteria and evidence. For justify, support the argument or conclusion with reasons from the case. For analyse, show the parts, their relationships and what follows.
